text:
Rox built its Revenue Agents business on Global 2000 companies, $5T+ in combined market cap by their count. That's backwards from how software usually spreads.

New tools normally enter through small teams and climb to the enterprise. SaaS worked that way, and so did most of the modern sales stack. Agents inverted the curve, and the reason is mundane.

Getting an agent to run a real pipeline in production takes revenue-specific context on your accounts, harnesses around the CRM and the inbox, and usually forward-deployed engineers to wire the whole thing together. Global 2000 names like MongoDB, Together AI, and Xbow have the engineering bench for that. Most sales teams have zero engineers to spare, so the teams that would benefit most from an extra set of hands were the ones locked out.

The budget shift already happened at the top of the market. Ishan says those same enterprise buyers moved investment from legacy CRM and SaaS into Revenue Agents over the past two years. What was missing was a version of the agents anyone could turn on.

Rox Teams, launched today, is their swing at that setup problem. The pitch is the same agents with the setup baked into the product, self-serve and live in minutes. The pricing reads like a real push down-market. It starts free, then charges for agent work, with individuals at $100 a month and teams at $255 with unlimited seats.

The question underneath the launch is where all that setup work went. Context engineering was the hard part for a reason, and Rox is claiming to have folded it into the product itself. If that holds, the adoption curve snaps back to bottom up, and the most interesting revenue agent stories of the next year will come from teams too small to have ever hired an FDE.

Congrats @ishanmkh and the @rox_ai team.

text:
somewhere in SF a Salesforce exec is genuinely SCARED for the first time in a decade...

because this is the end of their moat: the interface

it makes zero sense for a human to spend the day inside a CRM doing maintenance: researching accounts, logging calls, updating fields, chasing renewals

so these guys decided to put agents directly on top of the Salesforce database, one agent per account, all working from the same data, and the agents do the job the interface was built for:

> research: every account gets assembled from emails, calls, product usage, CRM history and what's happening on the web, before a rep touches it

> outreach: the agent writes and runs the sequences on that context, not on a template

> deals: it tracks every live opportunity, drafts the follow-ups and writes the updates back into Salesforce itself

> renewals: it watches the whole book and works every contract coming up, nobody has to remember

reps just tell it what they need in one sentence, it already knows the account better than they do
